en: *Essential Extracts from the Commentary on the Treatise on the Non-differentiation of the Dharma-realm*, Volume One.
Composed by the Great Master Guangyan Wujie, Puguang.
Our Patriarch, the National Preceptor Xianshou of Kāñcī, was personally summoned during the Chuigong era of the former Tang dynasty.
Together with the Tripitaka Master Ti-yun Prajñā of the Kingdom of Khotan, he translated this treatise;

once the task of transcribing was completed, he subsequently composed a commentary. His intention was to enlighten others regarding the three provisional means and to manifest the one ultimate reality, so that the teachings of Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna might be widely disseminated in his time and transmitted eternally without decay—this would indeed provide profound benefit to the source of transformation.

Although scholars who expounded the teachings and established their doctrines have appeared from generation to generation without fail, this commentary remained long concealed beyond the Liaodong Sea, with no reports of its circulation.
It was only during our Holy Song dynasty that it became unified; Prince Yu-se of Goryeo came to court, whereby these sacred texts were returned once more to China.
Since its phrasing and purport are lofty and profound—something not previously seen or praised by former masters—it is now brought forth.
There may be those who, wishing to delve into and admire this work, find their hands and feet at a loss for what to do.
Observing that I, an unworthy person, grasp the brush and hold the pen to mend its deficiencies, I have composed two volumes of annotated commentary.

I have prefaced it with a summary and titled it accordingly, so that future readers may grasp the essential and subtle meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and thereby provide resources for those who expound upon it. Furthermore, let it not be considered mere madness.

To simplify, I shall blame myself. The commentary (*śāstra*) is divided into two parts: first, the title; second, the exposition of the commentary. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the presentation of the title of the commentary, which consists of nine characters;

these represent two layers of "retaining and discarding" and "combining and separating" regarding the relationship between subject and object. First, both are retained: herein, the "commentary" (*śāstra*) serves as the subject that explains.

The "superior" refers to that which is understood; thus, the commentary (*śāstra*) is contrasted with the understanding. Regarding that which is understood, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* (the Treatise) is the signifier (*vācaka*), while all else is the signified (*vācya*).
Thus, the commentary is contrasted with the understanding that it clarifies, taking its name from the treatise it explains;

the signifying treatise is designated by the title of the signified meaning it conveys. Both follow the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound: "commentary" (*ṭīkā*) is so called because it elucidates (*vispaṣṭayati*) [the text].

"Deciding upon the meaning" (*niścaya-artha*) means that the commentary resolves the textual meaning so that there is no obstruction, just as one clears the blockages of rivers and streams so that the channels and marshes flow freely.
Because profound meanings and deep texts flow smoothly from this, it is named accordingly;
the commentary itself explains the title of the treatise being interpreted below.
The two characters at the beginning mark the author; the first two characters signify the name of the dynasty, and the following four characters indicate the name of the commentator.
"Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "diligent in cessation," which is the general designation for a disciple of the Buddha (śākyaputrīya).

It refers to one who diligently cultivates morality, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*), and quiets the afflictions, karma, and suffering (*kleśa-karma-duḥkha*)—that is, one whose name signifies the production of goodness and the extinction of evil. "Fǎzàng" (Dharmatara) refers to the commentator.
To have a name at birth and to treat it with reverence after death is the custom of this land. This refers to the third patriarch of the Avataṃsaka school, whose name was Zifu.
He was praised as being born from a lotus in his causal stage like Amitābha, and extolled for his realization of the nature of reality like Vairocana.

His life was like the sun shining upon a high mountain, according to the epitaph composed by Yan Gong, the Secretariat Director of the Tang Dynasty. His secular surname was Kang, a family of many generations.

According to tradition, he was the ancestral patriarch of the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Kangju. His grandfather came from Kangju to pay court, and his father, Mi, was posthumously honored by the Imperial Court as Left Attendant-in-Ordinary.
When Shuzhu was only sixteen years old, he refined one of his fingers before the Śāriputra Stūpa of King Aśoka to offer it as an act of devotion.

Thereafter, he traveled to Mount Taibai, where he deeply admired the profound mystery of the Dharma. Upon hearing that Master Yan of Yunhua Temple was lecturing there, he went to attend his teachings.
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he served as the primary attendant (upādhyāya), receiving the pouring of water into the flask;
through the causal conditions of this act of offering milk into the water, his fame spread throughout the world and his reputation reached the very limits of the earth.

Having repeatedly received imperial edicts, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda from Khotan, Bodhiruci, and others, he fully translated various sections of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Pitakas, as well as commentaries on these treatises.
The Chief Editor was Shou, who once lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* up to the "Worthy Head" (*Xianshou*) chapter. Thereupon, five clouds gathered in the sky and the earth shook in six ways.
He was granted the title National Preceptor Xianshou. His system for classifying the teachings followed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, uniquely capturing its profound mysteries;

his commentaries were comprehensive and circulated throughout the world, such that he became known as the founder of the Xianshou school of doctrine. Other details are recorded in separate biographies composed by eminent figures.

The *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states: "To 'create' (*zao*) means the sense of fabrication or composition. To 'expound' (*shu*) principles refers to describing what has existed from the past.
Because this treatise was newly composed, it is termed 'creation. Yet, because it is created anew to serve as a gift of Dharma, the term 'expounding' (*shu*) is used to demonstrate humility."

Part Two: Exposition of the Commentary. This has two sections: first, an introductory discourse on the general purport; second, the opening of chapters for the formal explanation. Within the first section, there are three parts:
first, the presentation of the essence of the doctrine to be explained (*sūtrita-artha*); second, the demonstration of the causes and conditions for the means of expression (*vācaka*);

third, a brief explanation of the essential points of the title. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, clarifying the non-obstruction between nature and conditions; second, revealing the profound and vast nature of the essence. Within the first of these, there are again two parts. First:

To provide a general explanation based on its nature, there are two parts. First, regarding the essence as transcending names and words: "Examine" (*xiáng*) refers to the beginning of entering the text and the starting point of initiating speech;

"examine" means to scrutinize with reality, while "verily" (*fú*) is a particle used to introduce speech. Now, when a person does not speak, their words, if spoken, must hit the mark; one must first examine and scrutinize before speaking.
The "Ocean of Nature" (*xìng-hǎi*), being void and quiescent, serves as a pointer to the Dharma-body—that is, the very subject of this treatise.

The nature of the fundamental dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the true nature of all phenomena; it is called the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), and is also called the "dharma-realm," or "suchness" (*tathatā*) and the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because it possesses these virtues, the ocean is used as a metaphor. Since this is a synthesis of the metaphor and the reality, it is termed the "ocean of nature.

"Vast" means that its essence is not material or obstructive; "congealed" means that its nature is without change or variation. This briefly reveals the virtues of the essence of the Dharma. This is the name.
Thus, the words that express the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena are themselves merely language—namely, vocal sounds, the path of speech, vocal karma, and vocal intimation.

Fundamentally, there is no such thing as "words" or "names," for they are beyond the reach of language. Now, to say that [the ultimate] transcends them is like casting away the trap and the snare once the fish and the hare have been caught;
as the *Yi Zhou Lue Li* says: "Words arise from images, therefore one may seek the images by following the words; images arise from intention."
Therefore, one may seek the image to perceive the meaning, and the meaning is fully expressed through the image; the image is made manifest through words.

Thus, one attains the meaning and forgets the image, and attains the image and forgets the words. This is just as the snare exists for the sake of the rabbit, yet once the rabbit is caught, the snare is forgotten;
or as the fish-trap exists for the sake of the fish, yet once the fish is caught, the trap is forgotten. Consequently, words are the snare for the image, and the image is the [trap] for the meaning.
The fish-trap exists for the sake of the fish; those who cling to the words do not grasp the image. The image exists for the sake of the meaning;
those who cling to the image do not grasp the meaning. Since the image arises from the meaning, if one clings to the image, what is retained is no longer the image.

Since the word arises from the image, if one clings to the word, what is retained is no longer the word. [Wenzi] He says: "The trap and the snare are themselves these names and words"—this may also be so.

It is not that there is a separate state of quiescence apart from the mind; rather, it is the very nature of the mind that is inherently quiescent. This is called the gate of the quiescence of the mind. Furthermore, because this mind is fundamentally empty and still, it is devoid of all marks of arising and ceasing; this is called the gate of the quiescence of phenomena. This refers to what is called "the greatness of essence" (*tattva-mahatva*). The *Treatise on the Great Meaning* states: "First, the greatness of essence means that the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This thus simultaneously possesses both the two objects of entry and the two gates of entry. Regarding the "two dharmas":
first, the Mahāyāna as the differentiation of immeasurable and boundless phenomena, which neither increases nor decreases; second, the quiescent [Mahāyāna]... [text fragment ends].

The Mahāyāna is a single flavor, equal, neither increasing nor decreasing; now, it is merely called "quiescence" because the phrasing is concise. It clarifies the latter [gate] and indicates the former by shadowing it;
this refers to the functional meaning of the gate, namely, that which is able to enter. Because noble wisdom traverses it universally, it is called a "gate. There are two such gates:
the so-called "gate of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-dharma*) and the "name-gate," which are likewise identical; therefore, they are simply interchanged.
Within the Dharma, the Mahāyāna is taken as the gateway; its response is without fixed direction and is thus called "perfect response" (*yuán-yìng*).

By virtue of the three great meanings, it is three yet one, and one yet three; since raising one fully encompasses all, it is said that they are "latent and pervasive" in both aspect (*xiàng*) and function (*yòng*).
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* states: "Second is the greatness of aspect (*xiàng-dà*), which refers to the Tathāgatagarbha being replete with immeasurable inherent merits."
By virtue of its qualities, it likewise possesses both the two dharmas and the two gates. Regarding the two dharmas: first is the Mahāyāna of the Tathāgatagarbha’s qualities;
second is the Mahāyāna of the fully endowed nature-qualities. The two gates are also like this, as can be understood by analogy with what precedes.

As for their function, the *Dacheng Yizhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna) states: "Third is the Greatness of Function (*yòngdà*), which refers to the capacity to give rise to all mundane and supramundane phenomena."
Because of the wholesome causes and effects of the world, one likewise possesses both dharma-gates. As for these two dharmas:
first is the Mahāyāna that can produce all worldly causes and effects; second is the Mahāyāna that can produce all supramundane wholesome causes and effects.
Within this context, the two gates are analogous to the preceding ones.
Second, regarding the two [aspects], the lower section distinguishes them by way of their conditions. First, it承接 (jìngché) the preceding to initiate the subsequent;
second, it clarifies the absence of obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*) in entering and exiting. Thus, the word "by" (*yóu*) serves to承接 (jìngché) the preceding. It is not the case that it is otherwise;
for the profound ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) previously elucidated is serene, eternally abiding, and inconceivable. This inconceivable cause is summoned as the "wondrous cause."

This is also called the "causal Buddha-nature" (*hetu-buddhadhātu*). Although it is serene, eternally abiding, and unchanging, it is able to follow conditions (*pratyaya*) to manifest all phenomena, just as the great ocean serves as the deep reservoir for waves and surges. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"It is like the vast ocean waves, which arise from a fierce wind; the great billows surge through the depths of the sea without interruption."
The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* abides eternally, yet it is stirred by the winds of objective spheres (*viṣaya*), causing the various waves of consciousness to surge and arise.
Regarding the statement that "all phenomena arise from conditions": all dharmas arise entirely from causes and conditions;

since the karmic causes that induce them and the resultant consciousness they attract are both unreal, they are said to be illusory fruits. This is just like a magician who performs various magical feats—all such things are likewise [illusory].
Because all phenomena, such as the various illusions of karma, cause, and effect, arise and cease only by depending upon nirvāṇa, the subsequent verse states:
"Just as all worlds arise and perish depending upon space, so too do the sense faculties arise and cease depending upon the unconditioned."

Second, the section on "Entering and Exiting" correctly elucidates non-obstruction. This has two parts: first, the general heading, which consists of two phrases; second, the explanation, which is as follows:
First, "exiting" refers to the arising of delusion from the True [Suchness], while "entering" refers to returning to the True from delusion.
As the *Vyākhyā-mahāyāna-śāstra* quotes the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, where at that time the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha..."
I recall that in the past, during the process of emergence, I came to rely upon the other, and during the process of entry, the other came to rely upon me.

This treatise cites this to establish the meaning of the two modes of turning: "during the process of emergence, I come to rely upon the other" refers to the downward-turning gate (*adhaḥ-pravṛtti-mukha*);
"during the process of entry, the other comes to rely upon me" refers to the upward-turning gate (*ūrdhva-pravṛtti-mukha*). Here, "I" refers to *tathatā* (suchness).
The Tathāgata-garbha of original enlightenment is said to "receive perfuming" in the sense that it turns its back on its own fundamental essence and, depending on ignorance, emerges into the other.
Thus, when it follows along with defilement, it is called the "downward turning"; when it returns to purity, it is called the "upward turning.

These two types of emergence refer to emerging provisionally to transform sentient beings, while entry refers to entering into realization and verifying the principle. However, both of these meanings are such that emergence pertains to phenomena (*dharma*), whereas entry pertains to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Thus, principle (li) establishes phenomena by depending on principle; therefore, phenomena and principle are fused, and because the phenomena of the dharmas are identical to principle, they coincide with phenomena.
For this reason, it is said that "entering and exiting are a profound union. In the subsequent phrase, movement is also phenomenon and stillness is also principle;
because they mutually integrate without obstruction, it is called "harmonizing."

Second, the principle does not descend to a separate explanation of the two [aspects]. This section has two parts: first, the formal clarification; second, a further explanation of the preceding. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections.

First, regarding "the principle of following conditions from the nature does not contradict the phenomena," this means that because the unchanging is itself the following of conditions, the principle does not conflict with the phenomena.
That is to say, because of the unchanging, there is the following of conditions; thus, the nature does not transform to become a thing. This establishes the reliance on the principle mentioned above.
Regarding the meaning of "accomplishing phenomena" (*siddha-vastu*): "The two matters do not descend; phenomena follow from nature and do not deviate from principle.

This means that because following conditions is itself non-changing, phenomena do not deviate from principle. Because that which arises through conditions necessarily lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one does not destroy phenomena to return to nature.
This establishes the aforementioned meaning that phenomena are identical with principle. The latter [passage] is as follows:
Below, the passage "the nature is not self-nature, etc. further explains the preceding text "the principle does not contradict the phenomena, etc.
by means of the meaning that nature follows conditions; and the passage "things are not other things, etc. further explains the preceding text "the phenomena do not contradict the principle, etc.
by means of the meaning that conditions follow nature.
Second, "thereby one knows" and below reveals that the substance and magnitude are profound and vast. First, "containing within it the Great Void" means it broadly encompasses the boundless;
"concealing even the finest speck of dust" means it subtly enters the infinitesimal. This is the restatement of the preceding terms. Following this, "in reality, only...
and below concludes by attributing [the nature] to establish the meaning of the unimpeded nature and conditions mentioned above.

Section Two: Distinguishing and Demonstrating the Means of Expression (*vyañjana*). This section has two parts: first, lamenting delusion and the composition of the treatise; second, praising the profound meaning based on the expression.

Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, describing errors that deviate from the central tenet; second, identifying the person and praising their virtue; third, explaining the reasons for composing the treatise. Within the first of these, there are two further points:

first, the state of being obscured by worldly attachments and failing to fathom the truth; this refers to how the aforementioned principle of the unimpeded nature and conditions—the profound and ultimate intent—is misunderstood.
This subtle, supreme, and wondrous power of the cause is beyond the reach of intellectual discrimination by sentient beings.

Second, regarding those who cling to expedient means and lose the essential intent: it is said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this profound teaching and principle of the One Vehicle will decline and fall into ruin.
Consequently, some among the later students may instead preserve and cling to the teachings proclaimed through expedient means, refusing to hear or accept the teachings that accord with reality.
To discuss this as one who "guards the provisional while deviating from the real" is like the saying that "one may carry hemp while discarding gold"—it is indeed possible.

The second section, "The Standard for Persons and the Praise of Virtue," consists of the first phrase which identifies the person and the subsequent phrases which praise his virtue. Regarding "a preeminent figure" (*jie*), the *Shijing* says, "A preeminent figure of the state.
Here, it refers to this Bodhisattva, who was born in Central India and was at that time the sole peerless master in that land; therefore, he is called "preeminent. (See the sub-commentary below).
The *Yin-san-zang* (Introduction by Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang) states that according to tradition in the Western Regions, this master was a Bodhisattva of the Grounds (*bhūmi*).

Therefore, it is said that his rank had reached the realization of truth, and his virtuous deeds and reputation were spread throughout the Five Indias; he was thus a preeminent and extraordinary hero.
Regarding the threefold reflection on the reasons for composing this treatise, they are fully detailed below in the eighth section of the commentary.
Second, regarding the praise of the profound meaning based on the exposition of the text, there are two parts. First, the general indication of the broad outline of composing this treatise:
it is said, "This is the treatise," because this treatise is the exposition of the principles of the non-contentious wheel of Dharma of the One Vehicle;

it is not an object of conceptual discrimination through words and thoughts, and it utterly cuts off the clamor of various conflicting views. Therefore, it transcends the realm of emotional and intellectual speculation.

This is the trace of its grasping. Second, the specific praise of *bodhi* has two parts: first, the excellence of that which is expressed (*vācya*), and second, the function of that which establishes it (*vākya*).
Regarding the manifestation of the nature through cultivation, there are also two parts: first, the direct explanation; and second, the further explanation of "the sprouts of virtue" and so forth.
*Bodhicitta* is the cause that brings about accomplishment, while the realm of *nirvāṇa* is the fruit obtained. This means that by means of this treatise, [the nature] is first revealed.
Because it demonstrates the fruit of the bodhicitta, it is taught as the supreme ground of cause and effect. "Ground" (*bhūmi*) generally takes wisdom and principle as its essence;
because it serves as a support and causes [virtues] to grow, it is called a "ground. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"That is to say, within the ten grounds, one cultivates ten superior practices, eliminates ten heavy obstacles, realizes ten true suchnesses, and through these two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one attains realization. Thus it concludes.
Thus, these ten stages (*bhūmi*) collectively encompass the conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature;

because they serve as the supreme support for the practices being cultivated, enabling them to grow and flourish, they are called "stages. Because he is not bound by karma, he is not constrained by the power of karma. Because he is not constrained by the power of karma, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a person who, having obtained a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), can produce whatever they desire. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has cultivated the roots of goodness for a long time, he possesses great spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*). Because he possesses great spiritual power, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a skilled potter who, using clay, water, a wheel, and his hands, can fashion various vessels as he desires. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has attained the power of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), he is not subject to birth and death. Because he is not subject to birth and death, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a great physician who, possessing various medicines, can cure all illnesses as he desires. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he is free from all attachments. Because he is free from all attachments, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a master illusionist who, using various illusions, can manifest various forms as he desires. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has perfected the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), he possesses immeasurable merit and virtue. Because he possesses immeasurable merit and virtue, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a great king who, possessing a vast treasury, can bestow wealth upon others as he desires. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he is beyond all conceptualization. Because he is beyond all conceptualization, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like the wind, which moves through empty space without obstruction. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has severed the continuity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), he is no longer subject to rebirth. Because he is no longer subject to rebirth, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a lamp whose oil is exhausted; once extinguished, it cannot be lit again. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the ultimate truth of the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-satya*), he is eternally at peace. Because he is eternally at peace, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a person who has reached the other shore of a great river; they are no longer troubled by the current. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has attained the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), he is irreversible from the path to Buddhahood. Because he is irreversible from the path to Buddhahood, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a mountain peak that cannot be shaken by the wind. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has perfected the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*), he possesses the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). Because he possesses the power of wisdom, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a great general who, leading his army, can conquer all enemies as he desires. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the nature of all phenomena as being empty and quiescent, he is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Because he is free from all conceptual proliferation, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like the sky, which is vast and open, beyond all description. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has attained the power of the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśa-tathāgata-bala*), he is invincible. Because he is invincible, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a diamond (*vajra*), which cannot be broken by any other substance. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the equality of all dharmas (*sarva-dharma-samatā*), he is free from discrimination. Because he is free from discrimination, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like the sun, which shines equally upon all things without partiality. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has perfected the cultivation of the four immeasurables (*catvāry-apramāṇāni*), he possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because he possesses great compassion, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a mother who loves her child; she would endure any hardship to protect them. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the non-arising of all dharmas (*anutpāda-dharma*), he is free from the cycle of birth and death. Because he is free from the cycle of birth and death, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a dream; once awakened, there is nothing to be found. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has attained the state of the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*), he knows all things without obstruction. Because he knows all things without obstruction, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a mirror, which reflects all forms clearly and without distortion. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the ultimate truth of the cessation of suffering, he is eternally liberated. Because he is eternally liberated, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a fire that has been extinguished; its heat is gone, and it cannot burn again. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has perfected the cultivation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), he possesses mastery over form and formlessness. Because he possesses mastery over form and formlessness, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a skilled painter who, using colors and brushes, can create various beautiful images. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has realized the nature of all dharmas as being like an illusion, he is free from all delusion. Because he is free from all delusion, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a magician who, using spells and incantations, can manifest various illusory forms. For this reason, it is said that an Arhat can dwell in the realm of empty space and fulfill the Buddha-way. Furthermore, because he has attained the power of the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), he is fearless in preaching the Dharma. Because he is fearless in preaching the Dharma, he can manifest his body according to his will. It is like a lion, the king of beasts
Those born in the three realms of existence who emerge from them into a pure buddha-field will not even have the name of "affliction" there;
in that land, they shall hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* from the Buddha and fully perfect the path to buddhahood.

As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there may be arhats who, having not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, claim for themselves that they have attained final nirvāṇa. For their sake, I shall preach this matter in other lands. You [should know this].
"All shall become Buddhas. The commentary states: "The text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is clear and accords with this sub-commentary;

thus we know that although Śrāvakas have emerged from the three realms, they possess their own lands where they will certainly turn their minds toward Buddhahood, rather than entering into eternal extinction.
Next, the cited treatise is that composed by Vasubandhu. Regarding the "Bodhisattvas who receive predictions," this refers to the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta.
While on the road, the Bodhisattva universally prostrated to the fourfold assembly and said, "I do not slight you;

you all practice the path of the bodhisattva, and you shall all become Buddhas. At that time, monks, nuns, and laymen and women of overweening pride beat and reviled him, saying, "We do not accept this false prediction [of enlightenment]. The commentary on that [sūtra] explains: "These people of overweening pride..."

Because the faculties of the śrāvakas were not yet mature, the Tathāgata did not bestow a prediction upon them himself; rather, it was a bodhisattva who conferred the prediction of enlightenment as a skillful means to inspire their initial resolve.
Based on this, there is no fixed nature [of their destiny]. Now, this commentary briefly extracts and cites that meaning, further stating:

"As for his [the Buddha's] use of the various dhyānas," the explanation says: "The two vehicles, though lacking a remainder-body, still pass through the extinction samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) despite its cessation."
It is for the sake of skillful means that they speak of "all dhyānas.
In the second, fourth, and seventh fascicles of the ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it is stated in identical terms that the two vehicles have no real nirvāṇa;
rather, it is solely through the power of samādhi that they will eventually attain unsurpassed bodhi. Since it is said that [nirvāṇa] does not exist...
In reality, the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is identical to the single nature of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the first part of the *Ghanavyūha-gāthā*, there are two sections: first, the citation of the text; second, the explanation of its meaning. Both are teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Transformation death (*pariṇāmika-maraṇa*) refers to the mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power.
Second, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it not only establishes through scriptural testimony that transformation death truly exists, but also...
It also clarifies that those of the two vehicles fundamentally have no *nirvāṇa*.

In the initial citation of the text to establish this point, first the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is cited, and then the *Mūla-śāstra* is cited to clarify the absence of the two types of *nirvāṇa*.
Second, from this point downward, the meaning and intent are summarized and demonstrated.

Regarding the two [sections on] the essence of the five teachings, first, the chapter title is cited to provide a general indication; second, based on that indication, there is a detailed explanation. First, the gate of according with phenomena (yathā-vastu-mukha).

Within this, first is the enumeration of the items, followed by their selection and differentiation. Regarding the former [the enumeration], first is the heading, and second, "Alternatively, below" is the specific illustration, which consists of four parts.
First, [it is shown that] there are only names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*). First, the names, phrases, and phonemes are established and defined;

second, their sequential arrangement, their systematic placement, and their successive conjunction constitute the basis for expressing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*).

Because they are the basis [for expression], sound (*ghoṣa*) is the support, not the actual substance of the teaching, as it is merely an indirect cause. That is to say, speech gives rise to names and so forth, and names and so forth are then able to manifest [the meaning].

Regarding the meaning of these three: although they are not distinct entities apart from sound, they differ as conventional and real, nor are they identical to sound, because their essence follows their function.
Therefore, it is said that the objects [of the two knowledges] are distinguished: the first (the knowledge of dharmas) takes the two—names and so forth—as its object, which is consciousness-only;

the second (the knowledge of expressions) takes real sounds and so forth as its object. Thus, the distinction of the objects is stated, even though both take the real as their object, for while the two are self-identical...

Because the nature [of the object] and its mutual inseparability are designated in relation to the signified meaning, they are termed "names" (*nāman*); because they mostly correspond to the capacities of sentient beings, they are called "sounds" (*śabda*).

Since the mind understands the meaning only after hearing the sound, these two are said to differ based on their distinct referents; it is not that there is a difference in their essential substance (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, these two objects, along with names and so forth—the three factors—when distinguished from sound, are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, because there are distinctions, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the sense-base of sound (*śabda-āyatana*), the sense-base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*), the element of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), and the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*) respectively subsume two categories:
sound and name, or simply voice and phoneme, as previously stated below (the subsequent cases are all to be judged accordingly).

"Voice" refers to the Buddha’s proclamations, discourses, and the sounds of speech (such as the musical scales of *gong* and *shang*), the pathways of speech (the domain where speech operates), vocal action (the function of speech), and vocal intimation (producing understanding in others).
This means that while the names, phrases, and syllables of the Buddha’s teaching merely manifest the function of the Buddha’s teaching, they are not its essence.

Because sound is real while names and so forth are conventionally established, and because names and so forth do not exist apart from sound—taking the conventional back into the real—all the cited treatises prove that sound constitutes the essence of the Buddha’s teaching.
Alternatively, both may constitute its nature, as both of the aforementioned explanations are valid.

This is because the scriptural teachings (*āgama*) serve as valid authority (*pramāṇa*). The ear takes the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) as its object, while the mind takes the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as its object;

it is only through these two objects that one attains hearing and understanding. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Sage’s collection of Dharma-aggregates (*dharma-skandha*) numbers eighty thousand. Its substance is either speech or names;

this is subsumed within the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), thus preserving both. Fourth, both [the ear and mind] may be neither [substantial], for the terms "sound" and "name" depend upon conditions.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, these two things are empty; furthermore, because they mutually negate one another, they form a statement of "neither-nor.

One may also cite the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) to prove that both exist and possess both [aspects]. Here, however, we take their mutual non-existence to manifest their very emptiness;
thus, the conclusion below states: "This is precisely 'not speaking' which is 'speaking.'"

Thus, all the holy scriptures arise from suchness; as the *Tattvārthāvatāra-śāstra* states: "That which is free from verbal expression, etc., is the nature of suchness (*dharmatā-tathatā*)."
To be free from the three provisional characteristics and to fulfill the three real virtues means that all verbal expressions lack reality, all provisional names lack reality,
and all mental consciousness merely follows deluded thoughts and is ultimately unobtainable.

Second, the explanation of the title has two parts. First, the general explanation of the Mahāyāna to distinguish its specific doctrine:

according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Hīnayāna is designated as the "half-syllable" teaching, while the Mahāyāna is designated as the "full-syllable" teaching. The doctrine adhered to by this treatise is exclusively the Mahāyāna.
Question: Why does the title of this treatise not directly designate "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) to universally exclude the provisional and the Lesser Vehicles, rather than using "Mahāyāna"?

Would this not lead to confusion with the provisional teachings of other schools? Answer: Although this [title] generally designates "Mahāyāna," it subsequently mentions "Dharmadhātu" and so forth, which clearly reveals the "one true meaning" (*eka-tattvārtha*) that is the primary tenet of this work.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The Dharmadhātu distinguishes and determines its meaning; this is the preceding tenet. Thus, the title serves as a general designation for Mahāyāna, while the specific content clarifies the intended doctrine.

The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as explained by the various masters each possesses two meanings, encompassing both cause and fruit; however, this treatise primarily elucidates the single vehicle (ekayāna) and the single nature (eka-svabhāva).
Thus, in both the stages of cause and fruit, the Dharma-realm is equal, of a single flavor, and without distinction;

this is precisely what reveals its intended meaning. As for the analysis of that which is expounded: because it analyzes principles with subtle precision, it is termed a "treatise" (śāstra), meaning an exposition.
Below, the established name is concluded as "Mahāyāna Dharmadhātu," and so forth.
Second, regarding the detailed explanation of the two [aspects], first is the explanation of the individual titles. Third, regarding Mahāyāna: first, the combined explanation of "Mahāyāna.
"Mahā" (Great) refers to its own essence as the title; it is distinct from provisional schools, and by selecting the name "Great" to exclude the "Small," there is "Small" outside of "Great."

How could that which is selected [as "great"] truly constitute the ultimate Great? What is now meant by "the essence itself" is that it does not depend upon or contrast with the small; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Because it does not depend on the emptiness of the small, it is called the Great Emptiness. Nirvāṇa is likewise: because it does not depend on the characteristics of the small, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.

This refers to the essence of this Dharma, which has no boundaries, transcends all measures, is cut off from the path of language, and is extinguished where the movements of the mind reach their limit.

The strong designation "Great" (Mahā) is used for two reasons: first, the sense of permanence (*nitya*), meaning that it vertically exhausts the three periods of time—having neither beginning nor end—and there is not a single phenomenon prior to it; because this alone precedes all phenomena, it is called "Great.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is called 'Great' is termed 'permanent. Second, the sense of pervasiveness, meaning that it horizontally encompasses the ten directions.
If one exhaustively searches the ten directions, there is no limit or boundary. As for what is called "Great" (*mahā*) in *Nirvāṇa*, its nature is vast and expansive, just like empty space.
Since this dharma-body extends vertically through time and pervades horizontally across space, there is nothing it does not encompass and nothing it does not pervade.

It is simply by speaking of its "encompassing" that the meaning of its "pervasion" is revealed. If the substance itself did not pervade, how could it be called "encompassing"? And if it did not encompass, how could it [be so]?
It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it encompasses all; this is the meaning of "Great. To explain this through analogy:

just as worldly boats and carts have the function of transporting heavy loads over great distances and are therefore termed "vehicles" (*yāna*), so too does the practitioner ride upon this Great Dharma to cross the wilderness of birth and death, traverse the river of afflictions, reach the land of Bodhi, and ascend to the shore of Nirvāṇa. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says:

Third is the transformation of cultivation, which refers to the stage of cultivation; because one repeatedly cultivates the practices of the ten stages, one gradually abandons the innate [afflictions].
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains that the transformation through penetration (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*) occurs in the first six stages,

wherein the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*) manifests intermittently as one penetrates the ultimate and conventional truths; because this causes the real and the unreal to alternately appear and not appear,
it is called the transformation through cultivation (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*), which occurs in the final four stages where the contemplation of signlessness manifests continuously for a long duration.

Through valiant cultivation, one eliminates the remaining *dauṣṭhulya* (coarse heaviness) so that what is not real no longer appears; this is the transformation into the perfection of the four fruits.

This refers to the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), when, through practicing boundless and difficult supreme practices over three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, whereby all primordial *dauṣṭhulya* is forever severed and Buddhahood is suddenly realized.

The perfection of the fruit is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that reaches the end of the future, providing inexhaustible benefit and happiness. The five inferior transformations refer to the stage of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

They exclusively seek their own benefit, loathe suffering, and aspire to quiescence; they are only able to penetrate the suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*), sever the seeds of afflictions, and realize true analytical cessation (*tattva-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because they lack superior capability, they are termed "inferior transformation. The sixth is the vast transformation, which refers to the Mahāyāna.
Because this state is for the sake of benefiting others, it proceeds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); it is devoid of both longing for *saṃsāra* and aversion to *nirvāṇa*.

It possesses the capacity to thoroughly penetrate the suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness, to simultaneously sever the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and to suddenly realize unsurpassed *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.

Because it has this superior capability, it is called the "Great Transformation" (*vipula-parāvṛtti*). [In this context,] the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and so forth are also explained in that same treatise.

The tenth [topic] explains the distinct meanings of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which briefly comprise four types: First, the path that effects the transformation. This, in turn, has two aspects:

1. The path of subduing: this refers to subduing the force of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles so that they do not give rise to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the two obstacles.

This includes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths, as well as the three types of wisdom—the preparatory (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)—according to their respective applications, gradually [effecting the subduing].

The path that suddenly subdues those two and is capable of severing them refers to the path that can eternally sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles; this path is certainly not contaminated (*sāsrava*).
This is because it is not induced by the grasping at signs practiced previously through contaminated preparatory effort (*prayoga*), as such signs have not yet been extinguished;

nor is it induced by preparatory effort seeking what is to be realized, as that has not yet been accomplished. Regarding the two bases of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there are again two: first, the basis that maintains the seeds (*bīja-dhāra-āśraya*), namely—

The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), by virtue of this [nature], is able to maintain the seeds of both defiled and pure phenomena and serves as the support for these defiled and pure phenomena;
the Noble Path transforms it so that it abandons the defiled and attains the pure. Although other portions of the *paratantra-svabhāva* are also supports, they cannot maintain seeds;
therefore, they are not mentioned here. The two bases of delusion and awakening refer to True Suchness (*tathatā*), because it is able to act as the fundamental basis for both delusion and awakening.

Defiled and pure phenomena arise in dependence upon this [basis]; the Noble Path functions to cause one to abandon defilement and attain purity. Although other factors also serve as bases for delusion and awakening, they are not fundamental;

therefore, they are not mentioned here. Regarding that which is abandoned through transformation, there are two types: first, abandonment by means of what is to be severed (*prahātavya*). This refers to the seeds of the two obscurations (*āvaraṇa*);
when the true path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) manifests, the obstacles and their antidotes are in mutual opposition. Thus, those [seeds]...
It is said that "abandonment" refers to the state where [the seeds] are severed and never again accomplished; because those seeds are severed, they no longer manifest.

Furthermore, the false attachment to a self and phenomena, as well as the self and phenomena thus grasped—which do not correspond to deluded cognition—are also called "abandoned. By this, it is termed the abandonment of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

That which is discarded consists of the remaining seeds of the *sāsrava* (contaminated) and the inferior *anāsrava* (uncontaminated), which are manifested by the *vajropama-samādhi* (diamond-like concentration).
Because the previously induced, extremely luminous, and purely immaculate fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is not the basis for those [defiled states], they are all eternally abandoned.

Once those seeds have been discarded, the presently existing contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) and inferior uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)—likened to gold—are ultimately non-arising.

Since they never arise again, this is also called "abandonment. By this, it is termed the abandonment of inferior phenomena within *saṃsāra*. (This accords with the teachings of various schools which state that within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), four matters are abandoned.)

The contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) of birth and death are comprised of three categories: first, contaminated wholesome states; second, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles; and third, all neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena along with inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states—these together constitute four categories, as they are also abandoned by the diamond-like path (*vajropama-mārga*).
Fourth, that which is attained through transformation has two aspects: first, that which is manifested, namely Great Nirvāṇa.

Although this is inherently pure by nature from the beginning, it was not manifest because it was shrouded by adventitious obstacles; now, when the true Noble Path arises and severs those obstacles, it is made manifest.
Its manifest characteristic is called "attaining nirvāṇa," because it is provisionally designated based on suchness being free from hindrances; its essence is thus the pure dharmadhātu.

Regarding the "attainment" produced by these two [aspects], namely Great Bodhi: although the seeds capable of producing it have existed from the beginning, they do not arise due to the obstruction of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
By the power of the Noble Path, those obstructions are severed, causing [the fruit] to arise from the seeds.
Having attained awakening, this continuity persists until the end of the future; this refers to the mental states associated with the four wisdoms.
Third, paying homage to that [state]. Regarding the cause, first is the formal explanation, followed by the citation of examples from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
As it says therein, Maitreya said to Sudhana: "O son of good family, you have already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Megha addressed the youth Sudhana, saying: "I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Megha immediately descended from his lion throne and prostrated himself before Sudhana with his five limbs touching the ground;
thereafter, rising up, he praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, noble son! You are indeed able to set your mind upon *anuttara*..."
Regarding the *samyaksambodhicitta*: thus, the reason Megha pays homage to Sudhana is that the *bodhicitta* is the cause of Buddhahood and is able to extensively produce all meritorious qualities.
[Text] Subsequently, he further cites scriptural authority to demonstrate this superiority.
Second, the differentiation of the fruits, which has two parts: first, the division of chapters; second, the formal explanation of the middle and lower verses.

Regarding the first verse, there are three sections: first, the commentary on the ability to benefit the world; second, the analysis of the meaning, which consists of a heading followed by an enumeration;

third, the explanation of the three meanings. Within the first two [meanings], they concern the non-retrogression of benefiting others; the last one concerns the loss of self-benefit. Within the former, the first concerns reaching the fruit.
